content: Rat-bite fever is an acute febrile illness in humans caused by bacteria transmitted primarily by rodents, most commonly rats. The disease is caused by two distinct organisms: Streptobacillus moniliformis and Spirillum minus. In the United States, the majority of cases are due to S. moniliformis, while S. minus is more commonly associated with cases in Asia and Africa. Both bacteria are part of the normal respiratory flora of rats and can be transmitted to humans through rat bites or scratches. Infection can also occur without a reported bite or scratch, simply by handling an infected rat. Additionally, S. moniliformis can be transmitted through ingestion of food or drink contaminated with rat excrement, a condition known as Haverhill fever. Other rodents, such as mice and gerbils, may also serve as reservoirs. Person-to-person transmission has not been documented. Spirillosis Rat-bite fever caused by the gram-negative spirochete Spirillum minus is less common and is predominantly found in Asia, where it is referred to as Sodoku in Japan. Symptoms typically appear two to four weeks after exposure to the organism. The wound through which the bacteria entered often shows slow healing and significant inflammation. Fever associated with spirillosis tends to last longer and may recur over months in some cases. Joint pain and gastrointestinal symptoms are generally less severe or absent. Penicillin is the most commonly used treatment for this form of the disease. Streptobacillosis The streptobacillary form of rat-bite fever, also known as Haverhill fever or epidemic arthritic erythema, is a severe illness caused by Streptobacillus moniliformis. It can be transmitted either through a rat bite or by consuming contaminated food or beverages. After an incubation period of approximately 10 days, the disease begins with high fevers, chills, headaches, and polyarthralgia. A characteristic rash, which may be maculopapular or petechial, often appears, and arthritis of large joints may develop. The organism can be cultured from blood or joint fluid. If left untreated, the disease can be fatal in approximately 10% of cases due to complications such as malignant endocarditis, meningoencephalitis, or septic shock. Treatment typically involves penicillin or tetracycline. Pathophysiology The initial scratch or wound caused by a bite from a carrier rodent results in mild inflammatory reactions and ulcerations. These wounds may initially heal but can reappear with the onset of systemic symptoms. The incubation period for rat-bite fever ranges from 4 to 28 days. Risk Factors Individuals at higher risk for infection include those who work with animals in laboratories or pet stores, as well as people living in dwellings infested with wild rats. Pet rat owners are also at risk of contracting the disease. History and Symptoms Early symptoms of rat-bite fever are nonspecific and include fever, chills, muscle pain (myalgias), joint pain (arthralgias), headache, and vomiting. Within 2 to 4 days after the onset of fever, patients may develop a maculopapular rash on the extremities or septic arthritis. The incubation period typically ranges from 2 to 10 days. If untreated, severe complications may include endocarditis, myocarditis, meningitis, pneumonia, and sepsis. In rare cases, the disease can be fatal. The presence of fever, rash, and arthritis in individuals with a history of rat exposure strongly suggests a diagnosis of rat-bite fever. Physical Examination The combination of fever, rash, and arthritis in a patient with a history of rat exposure is highly indicative of rat-bite fever. Medical Therapy Rat-bite fever responds well to penicillin antibiotics. For patients allergic to penicillin, erythromycin or tetracyclines can be used as alternative treatments for streptobacillary or spirillary infections, respectively. Prevention Preventive measures include avoiding contact with rodents, thoroughly washing hands and face after any contact with rodents, and cleaning and applying antiseptics to any scratches or wounds caused by rodents.
